paper.title: Tracing the Dynamics of Refusal: Exploiting Latent Refusal Trajectories for Robust Jailbreak Detection

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7 and Appendices B (onset vs final token), C (ROI sensitivity), D (static RepE baselines), E (adaptive attack); A (training) and F (extra tracing plots) skimmed

claims.claim: In safety-tuned chat models the internal state that causes a refusal is built mainly at the tokens just after the harmful concept in a request, in the middle layers, rather than being concentrated in the final prompt token that refusal-direction methods usually read. Supported only if, when hidden states from a harmful prompt are patched into a minimally different benign prompt, single-token patches at the token after the harmful word trigger full refusals far more often than patches at the final token (roughly twice as often in middle layers) in two different 3B model families; and if, aggregated over dozens of prompt pairs aligned at the harmful word, the highest refusal-induction rates lie at the immediately following tokens in intermediate layers, with the effect weakening further along the sequence.
claims.decision_rule: Onset-token patch refusal rate ~2x final-token rate at TW=1 in middle layers for Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B; aggregated peak right after the anchor in intermediate layers with attenuation downstream.

claims.claim: A small white-box detector that reads the raw hidden states across a window of middle layers and all token positions, instead of a refusal direction read at the final token or averaged over the prompt, detects jailbreak attacks it was never trained on far more reliably than existing detectors. Supported only if, trained only on ordinary safety data with jailbreak prompts removed and thresholded at a 10% false-positive rate on a benign-but-alarming prompt set, it detects at least 85% of direct harmful prompts, prefilling attacks, GCG suffix attacks and AutoDAN attacks on each of three model families, while every compared detector (perplexity filter, gradient-based detection, a linear probe, randomised smoothing) falls below 70% on at least one attack and model; if refusal-direction readouts taken at the last token or averaged over tokens perform much worse under the same protocol; and if it still detects at least 80% of attacks from a white-box GCG adversary optimising against the detector itself.
claims.decision_rule: DSR >= 85% on Direct, Prefilling, GCG, AutoDAN for Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B at XSTest-10%FPR; each baseline < 70% somewhere; RepE-terminal/mean much worse; adaptive GCG DSR >= 80%.

experiments.text: Set up causal tracing for refusal. Setup: build minimal pairs of a harmful and a benign request differing only in a key word ('How to make a bomb?' vs 'How to make a cake?'); cache the harmful run's hidden states and patch the state at one layer-token position (over a sliding window of 3 layers) into the benign run; score with the cross-entropy of the refusal prefix 'I'm sorry' and count a success only when the generation is a full refusal, since some patches recover 'I'm' but continue benignly ('I'm happy'). Positions before the key word are identical in both prompts under causal attention and serve as a built-in null. Model Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for the case study.

Map where refusal is causally constructed. Setup: the single-pair case study, then 40 harmful-benign pairs of varied categories and syntax with traces aligned at the key word, reporting the share of patches that trigger refusal at each layer and relative position. Result: the key-word position is effective from shallow layers; the strongest effect appears at the token(s) immediately after it (e.g. '?'), negligible in shallow layers but peaking in intermediate layers; the effect then weakens across later positions, with a smaller resurgence at the last token; deeper layers take over as the relative position increases.

Compare patching just after the key word with patching the final token. Setup: 160 pairs on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, layer windows 1 and 3 and token windows 1, 3 and 6, measuring the refusal rate when patching starts at the post-key-word token versus the final token. Result: with token windows of 1 and 3 the post-key-word token is clearly more effective (Llama, 3-layer window, single token: peak above 0.6 vs about 0.3 for the final token); with a 6-token window the final-token patch slightly overtakes, because on short prompts its window reaches back over the post-key-word tokens.

Define the detector and the evaluation protocol. Setup: stack raw residual-stream states from a middle-layer window into a layer x token tensor (no steering direction or PCA); apply parallel 2D convolutions spanning 3 layers and 2, 3 or 5 tokens, batch norm and ReLU, global max-pooling over valid positions, concatenation, dropout and a linear output (under 20M parameters). Train on about 5,500 prompts from PKU-SafeRLHF and Toxic-Chat with jailbreak prompts and prompts over 400 tokens removed, so no evaluated attack family is seen in training. Evaluate on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: AUROC on XSTest, then a threshold frozen at 10% false positives on XSTest and detection rates on AdvBench direct requests, prefilling attacks, GCG and AutoDAN (250 prompts).

Compare with existing detectors. Setup: perplexity filter, GradSafe, a linear probe and SmoothLLM under the same frozen threshold. Result: the detector reaches 98.3-99.0% on direct, 98.8-99.4% on prefilling, 85.4-96.5% on GCG and 98.8-100% on AutoDAN across the three models, with XSTest AUROC 93.2-94.8. Each baseline fails somewhere: the perplexity filter catches all GCG but 0% of prefilling on Mistral and Qwen direct; GradSafe 0% on Qwen prefilling and 2.0% on Mistral AutoDAN; the linear probe 32.0% on Mistral AutoDAN and 64.2% on Llama GCG; SmoothLLM 1.6% on Mistral AutoDAN. Without defence, attack success leaves only 3.2-88.3% refused.

Compare with static refusal-direction readouts on the same layers. Setup: mean difference between unsafe and benign training representations within the same layer window, scoring each prompt by projection, read at the final token or averaged over tokens, with the same 10% false-positive calibration; Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Result: the final-token readout detects 0.38% and 0.0% of GCG attacks (and 13.27% / 50.38% of direct requests); the averaged readout flags all attacks but has near-random XSTest AUROC (48.75 and 47.49), so it cannot separate benign from harmful; the layer-token detector gets 85.4-88.3% GCG with AUROC about 94.7.

Ablate the detector's design on Llama-3.1-8B. Setup: point-wise kernels only instead of multi-width kernels; mean instead of max pooling. Result: point-wise kernels lower GCG detection from 85.4% to 80.0% (AutoDAN 98.0%); mean pooling lowers GCG to 75.4% and AutoDAN from 100% to 0% even after re-calibration, consistent with a sparse signal diluted by averaging.

Check sensitivity to the chosen layer window. Setup: shift and resize the layer window (Qwen 12-22, 10-15, 8-18; Llama 3-12, 5-18). Result: detection stays high when the window covers the middle layers (Qwen GCG 85.5-87.3%, AutoDAN 95.2-99.2%), but a narrow window lowers XSTest AUROC (86.0 for Qwen 10-15) and an early window lowers Llama GCG to 79.8% and AutoDAN to 90.8%.

Attack the detector directly. Setup: a white-box adversary with access to the model, detector and threshold runs GCG on a joint loss of producing a target harmful prefix plus 5 times the detector's score, on AdvBench prompts. Result: 84.3% of attacks are still detected; where evasion succeeds, optimisation distorts the prompt's meaning (e.g. a market-manipulation request turned into a question about 'pylint'), and harmful-output success falls to 7%. Encoded inputs such as Base64 that the model does not decode do not trigger the refusal pattern and are noted as a limitation.
